issues.issue: The remedies list names "Title VI," which is a mechanical error for Title VII of the Civil Rights Act in an employment agreement that elsewhere covers sex, race and pregnancy discrimination claims. The mistake creates doubt about the arbitrator's power to award Title VII remedies.

The notice deadline — written notice "as soon as possible after the aggrieved first knew, or should have known, of the facts giving rise to the claim" — sets no measurable period and no consequence for late notice. Whether a claim is time-barred under this sentence cannot be determined from its own words.

The closing sentence requires notice "within any statute of limitations as set forth in the law of the state in which the community is located," which cannot be squared with c007 and c013, which commit federal statutory claims (FMLA, ADEA, ADA) with their own federal limitations regimes to arbitration. A court would be asked whether state periods shorten federal claims.

Venue is fixed at "the town or city where the community where you work is located," a present-tense reference that has no application to a former associate whose employment has been terminated — the very disputes the Procedure principally covers (c002). The contract elsewhere uses the past tense ("have been working" in c013), sharpening the ambiguity.

The cost clause is internally garbled — fees "will be paid for us initially, but as provided by statute or decision of the arbitrator" — leaving it unclear whether the employer pays, whether "for" means "by," and on what standard the arbitrator may reallocate. The gloss that "all costs could after all is complete be paid by us or you" makes the associate's exposure to AAA and arbitrator fees indeterminate.

Review is limited to "the grounds specified in the U.S. Arbitration Act or other applicable law," a catch-all sitting against the specific statutory grounds and capable of reopening the scope of judicial review the sentence purports to close. What "other applicable law" adds to the FAA grounds is left open.

The promise that "under no circumstances" will an employee be retaliated against for invoking the Procedure sits against c019, which reserves the right of the facility to terminate "at any time for any lawful reason." A court would be asked whether this clause creates an enforceable exception to at-will termination or is merely a policy statement.

The at-will disclaimer — employment terminable at any time and "not for any specific or definite duration" — cannot be squared with c003, which recites that the arbitration promise was given in exchange for "your employment as our associate," or with c006's "as a condition of your employment here." The adequacy and continued existence of the consideration turn on reading the two together.

The integration clause declares this the "complete agreement" on mediation and arbitration superseding prior understandings, yet c010 makes the arbitration trigger depend on "the informal procedure as outlined in the Handbook" and c010 incorporates the AAA rules by reference. A court would have to decide whether those extrinsic documents survive the merger clause.

The non-reliance sentence is grammatically broken — "any representations, oral or written, on the subject or the effect, enforceability or meaning of this Agreement" — so what subject matter the disclaimer covers is unclear. It also excepts what is "specifically set forth in this Procedure" while purporting to govern representations about "this Agreement," two labels the document uses inconsistently.

The severability clause says nothing about what survives if a core term such as the fee-allocation clause (c016) or the burden-of-proof clause (c012) is held unenforceable, or whether the arbitration obligation itself then falls. A court asked to strike one of those terms would have to construe how much of the Procedure remains.

The waiver of "any constitutional or statutory right ... to have covered claims decided in a court of law before a judge or a jury" is stated flatly, but c008 preserves court access for equitable relief and other excluded claims and c017 contemplates court entry and review of the award. A court would be asked how wide the waiver truly is once those provisions are read with it.
